newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia retailing to slow, still boost GDP.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia retailing to slow, still boost GDP.

text.p: Australian retail trade should ebb in September after a two month shopping frenzy by consumers, but was still expected to give a sizeable boost to economic growth for the third quarter.

The figures, due out on Friday, are expected to show sales dipped 0.5 percent in September after gains of 1.1 and 1.0 percent in August and July respectively. But real sales for the quarter, adjusted for inflation, were seen rising 1.3 percent in a big turnaround from the 0.6 percent fall in the June quarter.
Such a jump would add around 0.3 point to the expenditure based measure of gross domestic product (GDP-E) for the quarter.
Combined with an expected contribution of around 0.7 to 0.8 point from net exports, GDP-E was already shaping up to top 1.0 percent compared to the meagre June quarter gain of 0.2 percent.
"Final consumption expenditure should make a solid contribution to growth in the September quarter," said GIO chief economist Akis Haralabopoulos.

"In fact, the result may be further bolstered by continued growth in expenditure on services which are not captured in the retail turnover data," he said. Private consumption expenditure makes about about 60 percent of GDP-E and retail sales makes up about 40 percent of expenditure.
He was at the top of the market range for the quarter expecting a rise in real sales of 2.1 percent, a result which would add about 0.5 point to GDP-E.
"Growth in retail turnover, contrary to some media reports and general retail sector grumbling, has been fairly healthy over the last few months," said Haralabopoulos.
This partly reflected relatively high levels of consumer confidence and reasonably healthy growth in household income, he said, and looked for sales to rise 0.3 peercent in September.
Most analysts, however, thought some pay-back was inevitable in September after four months of growth.

In particular, they noted the Bureau of Statistics had cautioned that the strength in August may have been due to Father's Day falling early, on September 1, so the demand associated with it would have come in August.
The seasonal adjustment factor for this affected September, when the socks and ties would normally have been bought, so August sales would have been boosted at September's expense.
"Basically, the seasonal factor would have knocked some of the strength out of September," said Anthony Thompson, an economist at HongKong Bank Australia.
He saw other reasons to expect a slowdown.
"Consumer sentiment eased in September and fell particularly sharply in relation to whether it was a good time to buy a major household item," he said.
Employment had also dropped a hefty 34,100 that month and stores had begun to wind back the price discounting which was thought to have boosted demand in the previous two months.

"We're going for a 0.7 percent fall in sales but I wouldn't be surprised to see it down 1.0 percent," said Thompson. "That would bring trend sales growth back to around 0.3 percent from 0.5, which is more in keeping with the other evidence on demand." -- Wayne Cole, Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
